title: Observability: logs, metrics, traces
tagline: The three signals, what question each answers, and how to connect them when something breaks.
why: Every debugging method from Day 6 depends on evidence, and in production the only evidence is what your system recorded before the fault happened. Logs, metrics, and traces each answer a different question, and knowing which one to open first is most of the speed. For an agent like Relay, the failures that hurt most return status 200, so you also need to know what to record beyond status codes.
objectives: Find every log line for one failed request using its request ID, across the API and the worker
Read a percentile table and explain why the average hid a problem
Read a trace waterfall and name the span where the time went
Write an SLO for one Relay flow and decide whether an alert should page someone
Choose what to record for each LLM call and agent step so silent failures become visible

blocks.text: A **log** is a timestamped record of one event, written by the code that saw it happen. A **structured log** writes each event as named fields, usually one JSON object per line, so a machine can filter and count lines as easily as you can read them.
Logs answer the question *what happened to this one request*. When a Relay customer says a reply never made sense, the log lines for that request are the closest thing you have to a recording of it.

blocks.title: Relay logs filtered on one request ID
notes: One filter on `request_id` pulls lines from both the API and the worker. The worker has the ID only because the API copied it into the job message.
The tool timeout is a warning, and the request still finished with status 200. A dashboard of 5xx errors would never show this failure.
Every field is queryable. You can count `msg="tool timeout"` per hour without writing a regular expression.
No line contains the prompt, the customer's email, or the order details. The IDs are enough to find those in the database when you need them.

blocks.caption: The same event, two ways
rows: Search text and hope the wording is consistent
Filter on an exact field value
A regex per message format, which breaks when wording changes
Noisier, though log viewers render the fields
Personal data embedded in free text
Different field names for the same thing across services
blocks.verdict: Use structured logs in any service you will debug in production. Agree on field names (`request_id`, `user_id`, `route`) across services so one filter works everywhere.

items: `debug`: detail for development, usually off in production because of volume.
`info`: normal milestones, such as a request finished or a job completed.
`warning`: something failed but was handled, such as a retried call or a tool timeout the agent worked around.
`error`: the operation failed and someone may need to act. If everything is logged as an error, nothing is.

blocks.text: The request ID is the thread

A **request ID** is a unique string assigned when a request enters the system and attached to every log line written while handling it. Create it at the edge, in nginx or the first service, and return it to the client in a response header such as `X-Request-ID`. Pass it to every downstream call and copy it into every queued job.

blocks.title: You cannot find the logs for a failed request
blocks.text: Check the three places an ID gets lost. The entry point never created one, a background job did not carry it, or a library logged through a logger that does not add it. Each gap turns an exact filter into a guess based on timestamps.
What never goes in a log

items: Secrets: API keys, passwords, session cookies, `Authorization` headers, signed URLs.
Personal data: emails, addresses, phone numbers, card numbers. Log an internal ID instead.
Full prompts and model responses that contain customer text, unless they go to a store with the same access rules as the database.

blocks.title: Logging the whole request object
blocks.text: A debug line that prints the incoming request also prints its `Authorization` header. Logs are copied to more systems, kept longer, and read by more people than your database, so one such deploy spreads every caller's token widely. Redact in the logging setup, so no single call site has to remember.

Logs are stored and often billed by volume. A service that logs every SQL statement or every streamed token can produce far more log data than useful signal, and some pipelines start dropping lines when they fall behind.

blocks.title: Keep every log line, or sample

options.name: Full capture
gain: No guessing about what was dropped
cost: Searches get slower as volume grows
options.choose: Choose this for errors, warnings, and anything touching money, such as refunds.

options.name: Sample routine lines
gain: Keeps a representative picture of normal traffic
cost: The one successful request you need may be gone
Counts from logs must be scaled back up
options.choose: Choose this for high-volume `info` and `debug` lines on healthy requests, while keeping every warning and error.

blocks.q: A customer's failed request returned the header `X-Request-ID: req_91bc`. What is the fastest way to see what happened?
options: Filter all services' logs on `request_id=req_91bc`
Search the logs for the customer's email address
Scroll the API logs around the time of the complaint
Open the error rate dashboard for that hour
blocks.explain: An exact filter on the request ID returns that request's lines from every service and nothing else. Searching by email depends on personal data you should not be logging, and scrolling by time mixes in thousands of other requests.

blocks.text: A **metric** is a number recorded at regular intervals and stored as a time series. Metrics are aggregated before they are stored, so they stay cheap however much traffic you serve. They answer *how much* and *how often* across all requests, and never what happened to one.

blocks.caption: The three basic metric types
rows: A total that only goes up
A current value that rises and falls
How many observations fell into each value range, called a bucket
Queue depth, database connections in use
Percentiles and the shape of the distribution
Graphing the raw total, which rises forever
Sampling too rarely and missing short spikes
Bucket edges that do not match your latency targets
blocks.verdict: Count events with counters, measure levels with gauges, and record durations with histograms so percentiles can be computed later.

blocks.caption: Two checklists for what to measure
rows: Anything that handles requests: the API, a worker
Resources: CPU, memory, a connection pool, a disk
Replies per second, share that fail, reply latency percentiles
Pool connections in use, requests waiting for one, connection errors
blocks.verdict: Use RED for every service and dependency, and USE for the resources behind them. **Saturation** means work waiting because the resource is full, such as requests queued for a database connection.

blocks.text: Percentiles, and why averages hide problems

The **p95** is the value that 95 percent of measurements fall below; the **p99** is the value 99 percent fall below. Latency is skewed: most requests are fast and a few are very slow. An average blends both into a number that describes nobody.

blocks.title: Relay latency by route, last hour
blocks.code:
route                   count     avg     p50     p95     p99
POST /tickets/{id}/reply    2,800   3.1 s   2.4 s   6.9 s   9.8 s
GET  /orders/{id}         48,000   45 ms   30 ms   90 ms  410 ms
GET  /health             360,000    2 ms    1 ms    3 ms    5 ms
notes: For replies, the average of 3.1 s sits between the typical request at 2.4 s and the slow tail, and describes neither.
A p99 of 9.8 s means about 28 replies in this hour took longer than that.
The average across all routes is about 28 ms, because health checks make up most of the count. That is the number that looks fine while customers complain.
Percentiles cannot be averaged. The p99 of two servers is not the mean of their two p99s; it must be computed from the combined histogram buckets.

blocks.title: The tail reaches more users than it seems
blocks.text: A Relay session makes many requests. If each has a 1 percent chance of landing beyond the p99, a session of 20 requests sees at least one slow request about 18 percent of the time. Day 13 returns to tail latency in depth.
Cardinality

Each unique combination of label values on a metric is a separate time series, and the number of combinations is its **cardinality**. `http_requests_total` labeled by route (20 values) and status (8 values) has at most 160 series. Add a `user_id` label with 50,000 users and it can reach 8 million.

blocks.title: A metric with exploding cardinality
blocks.text: Labels such as user ID, ticket ID, request ID, raw URL path, or full error message create a new series for almost every request. The metrics system slows down, its memory and bill climb, and some backends start dropping series. Keep labels to small fixed sets such as route template, status class, and model name, and put per-request detail in logs and traces.

blocks.q: Which label is safe to add to Relay's LLM call duration histogram?
options: The model name
The conversation ID
A hash of the prompt text
The customer's account ID
blocks.explain: Model names form a small fixed set, so the series count stays bounded. The other three take a new value for nearly every call, which multiplies the series count by the number of conversations, prompts, or customers.

blocks.prompt: During an incident, customers report 30-second waits, yet Relay's average latency graph stays near 600 ms. Name two ways both can be true.
blocks.answer: A small share of slow requests barely moves an average, especially one diluted by fast routes such as health checks. And if the duration is recorded only when a request completes normally, the requests that timed out never reach the histogram at all.

blocks.text: A **trace** is the record of one request's whole journey, built as a tree of **spans**. A span is one timed operation, such as an HTTP call, a database query, or an LLM call, with a start time, a duration, a parent span, and attributes. Every span in a trace shares one trace ID.
Logs say what happened and metrics say how often. A trace says *where the time went* inside one request, which is the question you have after a metric shows that something got slow.

blocks.title: One slow Relay reply as a waterfall
blocks.code:
trace 4bf92f35  POST /tickets/812/reply  9870 ms  status 200
start(ms)  dur(ms)  span
        0     9870  api POST /tickets/812/reply
        1        2    redis GET session
        4       18    postgres SELECT ticket, messages
       23     9790    agent.run
       23     2310      llm.call #1  in=5120 tok  out=96 tok  stop=tool_use
     2335     5004      tool lookup_order  ERROR timeout after 5000 ms
     2336     5000        postgres SELECT orders  (canceled)
     7341     2440      llm.call #2  in=5300 tok  out=310 tok  stop=end_turn
     9815        9    postgres INSERT message
     9826        3    queue publish send_email
notes: Indentation is the parent and child tree. `agent.run` takes 9,790 of the 9,870 ms, so everything outside it is noise.
Inside the agent, about half the time is one tool call that timed out. The two LLM calls together take about 4.7 seconds.
The child span shows where the tool spent its time: a Postgres query that ran until the tool gave up. Day 9 explains why such a query can be slow.
The request returned 200. The model received the tool error and answered without the order. Only the span status shows the failure.
The 41 ms after the last child span is time in the handler itself, such as building the response.

blocks.text: Context propagation

For spans from different processes to join one trace, each call must carry the trace ID and the parent span ID. This is **context propagation**. Between HTTP services it travels in a header, standardized by W3C as `traceparent`. Across a queue, the producer must write it into the job message and the consumer must read it back. Some libraries do this for you, and many setups miss it.

blocks.title: One trace across the API, the queue, and a worker

steps.label: Starts the root span
steps.detail: FastAPI instrumentation creates a trace ID, or continues one from an incoming `traceparent` header.
steps.fail: Without instrumentation at the entry point, each downstream span becomes its own unrelated trace.

steps.label: Calls Postgres and the LLM API
steps.detail: Database driver and HTTP client instrumentation create child spans. The LLM provider does not join your trace, so you see only your side of the call.
steps.fail: A long span with no children means the time was spent inside something you cannot see.

steps.label: Publishes a job
steps.detail: Writes the current trace context into the job message, next to the payload.
steps.fail: If the context is not written, the worker's spans form a separate trace with no link to the request.

steps.label: Picks up the job
steps.detail: Reads the context from the message and starts a span whose parent is the publish span.
steps.fail: A long gap between publish and consume means the queue was backed up, not that the code was slow.

steps.label: Sends the email
steps.detail: The email API call becomes another child span in the same trace.
steps.fail: An error here appears on the trace long after the customer's request finished.

steps.label: Receives and samples spans
steps.detail: Each service exports spans to a collector, which decides what to keep and forwards it to the tracing backend.
steps.fail: If the collector drops spans under load, traces arrive with missing pieces.

blocks.text: **OpenTelemetry** is a vendor-neutral standard and set of libraries for producing traces, metrics, and logs. You add its SDK and instrumentation packages for FastAPI, your HTTP client, and your database driver, and spans appear without hand-written code. A collector receives the data and forwards it to the backend you choose, so changing vendors does not mean re-instrumenting.

blocks.caption: Logs, metrics, and traces side by side
rows: How much, how often, how fast overall?
Where did the time go inside this request?
blocks.verdict: Use metrics to notice and size a problem, traces to find the slow or failing hop, and logs to read the details. Put the trace ID in every log line so you can jump from one to the other.

options.name: Keep every trace
cost: Storage and ingest cost grow with traffic
options.choose: Choose this when traffic is low, as in staging or a small internal tool.

options.name: Head sampling
gain: The keep decision travels with the trace, so kept traces are whole
cost: Decided at the start, before anyone knows the request will fail
Rare errors and slow requests are mostly discarded
options.choose: Choose this when traffic is high and you mostly need typical behavior.

options.name: Tail sampling
gain: Keeps every error and slow trace
cost: The collector must hold all spans until each trace ends
More infrastructure to run and size
options.choose: Choose this when you need the failures specifically and can run a collector that buffers traces briefly.

blocks.title: A trace with holes
blocks.text: If a trace stops at the API and the worker's spans are missing, check that the job message carries the trace context. If a span is long with no children, the time is inside something uninstrumented: a library call, a lock, CPU work, or a remote service.

blocks.q: In the waterfall above, which change would cut this reply's time the most?
options: Fix the slow `lookup_order` query
Switch both LLM calls to a faster model
Cache the Redis session lookup
Speed up the message INSERT
blocks.explain: The tool span is 5 of the 9.87 seconds and is also why the answer lacked the order. A faster model could shave part of the 4.7 seconds of LLM time but leaves the failure in place; the Redis and INSERT spans are milliseconds.

lessons.title: SLOs, alerts, and what to instrument first

blocks.text: An **SLI**, or service level indicator, measures what users experience as a ratio of good events to all events. An **SLO**, or service level objective, is the target for that ratio over a window. For Relay: 99 percent of replies succeed and finish within 15 seconds, measured over 28 days.

The **error budget** is what the SLO allows to go wrong. At 99 percent and 200,000 replies in the window, about 2,000 may be slow or fail. When the budget is nearly spent, you slow down risky changes; when plenty remains, you can ship faster.
Page on symptoms

blocks.caption: Alerting on what users feel versus what machines do
rows: Reply SLI below target for 10 minutes
Few, since it fires only when users notice
Many, since high CPU is often harmless
Every failure nobody wrote a rule for
Dashboards and tickets that help diagnosis
blocks.verdict: Page on symptoms. Keep cause metrics on dashboards, where you read them once a symptom alert tells you to look.

blocks.title: Alert fatigue
blocks.text: When most pages need no action, people learn to ignore them, and the real one gets acknowledged and forgotten. Every page should be urgent, actionable, and about something users feel. Anything else becomes a ticket or a dashboard panel. Review last month's pages and delete the rules nobody acted on.

items: Is it broken? The SLI against its target, at the top, for each user-facing flow.
Where? RED metrics per route and per dependency: Postgres, Redis, the LLM API, the queue.
Since when? A time axis with deploy and config change markers, so the start of the problem lines up with a change.

blocks.text: Instrumenting an LLM or agent service

blocks.title: What to record in Relay's agent, from the outside in

layers.name: Run (one customer reply)
layers.role: Outcome, total latency, number of steps, total tokens, and estimated cost.
layers.breaks: Runs that hit the step limit or end without an answer look like successes if you record only the status code.

layers.name: Model call
layers.role: Model name and version, input and output tokens, time to first token, total time, stop reason, retries, and error type.
layers.breaks: A truncated answer shows only as a max-tokens stop reason, which nobody sees unless it is recorded.

layers.name: Tool call
layers.role: Tool name, latency, success or error type, and the size of the result returned to the model.
layers.breaks: Tool errors returned to the model as text raise no exception, so error rates stay at zero.

layers.name: Retrieval
layers.role: Query latency, number of chunks returned, and their IDs and scores.
layers.breaks: Empty or irrelevant results produce confident wrong answers with no error anywhere.

layers.name: Dependencies
layers.role: RED metrics for Postgres, Redis, and the LLM API, including 429 responses.
layers.breaks: Provider throttling shows up as slow runs, because the client retries quietly.

blocks.title: Relay agent metrics, last 24 hours
blocks.code:
tool                  calls  errors   err%     p50     p95
lookup_order          8,210     412   5.0%  180 ms   5.0 s
issue_refund            940       3   0.3%  420 ms   1.1 s
search_help_center   11,300      12   0.1%   90 ms  310 ms

runs 6,020   steps/run p50 3  p95 9   hit step limit 41
input tokens/run p50 5.1k  p95 38k
notes: The `lookup_order` p95 equals the tool timeout, so at least 5 percent of its calls run until they are cut off. That matches its error rate.
Every one of those 412 errors happened inside a request that most likely returned 200.
The p95 of input tokens per run is about seven times the p50. A few long conversations drive a large share of cost and latency.
These metrics are labeled by tool name and nothing finer. Conversation IDs belong on spans and log lines.

blocks.title: Errors that do not look like errors
blocks.text: In an agent, a failed tool call usually becomes a message to the model, and the model works around it. The HTTP status stays 200, the error rate stays flat, and answer quality drops. Count tool errors, step-limit stops, and max-token stops as their own metrics.

blocks.title: What to instrument first
blocks.text: A request ID and trace ID in every log line comes first, because it connects everything else. Then the SLI for each user-facing flow, then RED for each dependency, then per-step agent metrics.

blocks.prompt: Relay's 5xx rate is flat at 0.2 percent, but the nightly eval pass rate fell from 85 to 74 percent after a deploy. Which instrumentation would have caught it the same day?
blocks.answer: A tool error rate by tool name, and counts of runs that stopped at the step limit or on max tokens. Both rise when tools fail quietly while every request returns 200. An SLI defined on answered replies, rather than on status codes, would show it too.

fieldGuide.symptom: Average latency looks fine, but users say replies are slow
causes: A minority of requests take a slow path that the average hides
Fast routes such as health checks dilute a service-wide average
Timed-out requests never get a duration recorded
fieldGuide.look: p95 and p99 per route, especially the reply route, over the period of the complaints.
fieldGuide.confirm: The reply route's p99 is far above its p50, and the slow requests share a route or a dependency.
fieldGuide.fix: Dashboard and alert on per-route percentiles or on an SLI. This needs histograms, which cost more to store than a single average.

fieldGuide.symptom: Cannot find any log lines for a request a customer reported
causes: No request ID created at the entry point
The ID is not returned to the client, so support cannot quote it
Background jobs do not carry the ID
fieldGuide.look: The response headers of a real request, and whether worker log lines contain a `request_id` field.
fieldGuide.confirm: API lines have the ID and worker lines for the same work do not.
fieldGuide.fix: Create the ID at the edge, return it in `X-Request-ID`, add it to the logging context, and copy it into every job message.

fieldGuide.symptom: On-call acknowledges pages without looking at them
causes: Alerts on causes such as CPU or memory that usually resolve themselves
Thresholds set too tight
Several rules firing for one incident
fieldGuide.look: Last month's pages, and which ones led to any action.
fieldGuide.confirm: Most pages were resolved with no change made.
fieldGuide.fix: Page on SLI symptoms; move cause alerts to dashboards and tickets. You will learn of some resource trends later, but through their effect on users.

fieldGuide.symptom: Metrics backend became slow and its bill jumped right after a deploy
causes: A label with per-request values was added: user, ticket, conversation, or request ID
Raw URL paths used as a label instead of route templates
fieldGuide.look: Series count per metric, and which labels each metric gained in the deploy.
fieldGuide.confirm: One metric's series count grew by orders of magnitude while others stayed flat.
fieldGuide.fix: Remove the label or replace it with a bounded one. Move the detail to logs and span attributes.

fieldGuide.symptom: Worker spans show up as separate traces with no parent request
causes: The trace context is not written into job messages
The worker starts a new root span instead of reading the context
fieldGuide.look: A raw job message on the queue: does it carry a `traceparent` or similar field?
fieldGuide.confirm: Messages lack the field, or the worker's first span has no parent ID.
fieldGuide.fix: Inject the context when publishing and extract it when consuming, or use instrumentation that does both for your queue library.

fieldGuide.symptom: HTTP 200 everywhere, but evals and customers say the agent's answers got worse
causes: Tools fail and the error is passed to the model as text
Runs end at the step limit or on max tokens
Retrieval returns nothing useful
fieldGuide.look: Tool error counts by tool, stop reasons, and step counts per run, before and after the change.
fieldGuide.confirm: One tool's error rate or the share of abnormal stop reasons rose when quality fell.
fieldGuide.fix: Fix the tool, and add these counts to the dashboard with an alert on their rate.

fieldGuide.symptom: The trace for the exact failing request you need is not in the tracing backend
causes: Head sampling kept a small random share and dropped this one
The collector dropped spans under load
fieldGuide.look: Sampling settings in the SDK and collector, and the collector's dropped-span count.
fieldGuide.confirm: The kept share matches the sampling rate, and errors are no more likely to be kept than successes.
fieldGuide.fix: Use tail sampling that keeps all errors and slow traces. It costs collector memory to buffer traces until they finish.

fieldGuide.symptom: A token, password, or customer email shows up in log search
causes: A debug line printed a whole request or config object
An exception message included the offending value
fieldGuide.look: The logger call that produced the line, and how many days the value has been exposed.
fieldGuide.confirm: The same field appears in many lines from one code path.
fieldGuide.fix: Rotate the secret first, then redact in the logging setup and purge the affected lines where possible.

fieldGuide.symptom: Log costs doubled, or log lines are arriving late or missing
causes: Debug logging left on in production
A new line inside a loop, such as one per streamed token
fieldGuide.look: Log volume by service and by message over the last week.
fieldGuide.confirm: One message or one service accounts for most of the growth.
fieldGuide.fix: Remove or sample the noisy line, keeping all warnings and errors.

glossary.def: A log line written as named fields, usually one JSON object per line, so it can be filtered and counted by field.
A unique string assigned when a request enters the system and attached to every log line and job created while handling it.
A metric that only increases, such as total requests. You read its rate of increase.
A metric holding a current value that can rise or fall, such as queue depth or connections in use.
A metric that counts observations into value ranges called buckets, from which percentiles can be estimated and combined across servers.
The value below which a given share of measurements fall. The p99 latency is the time that 99 percent of requests beat.
The number of distinct label combinations on a metric. Each combination is a separate time series with its own storage cost.
The record of one request's path through the system, made of spans that share a trace ID.
One timed operation within a trace, with a start time, duration, parent, status, and attributes.
Passing the trace ID and parent span ID along with each call or message, so spans from different processes join one trace.
Keeping only some of the telemetry. Head sampling decides when a trace starts; tail sampling decides after it ends.
Service level indicator: the share of events that were good from the user's point of view, such as replies that succeeded within 15 seconds.
Service level objective: a target for an SLI over a time window, such as 99 percent over 28 days.
The amount of failure an SLO allows in its window. Spending it fast is a signal to slow down risky changes.

apply.title: Make your own LLM calls findable and measurable
steps: Pick one entry point in your project, such as an eval case or an API route. Generate a short random ID for each run of it and add that ID to every log line it writes. Print one run's lines filtered by that ID.
For every LLM call, write one structured log line with the ID, model name, input tokens, output tokens, stop reason, and duration in milliseconds. Most LLM APIs return token usage in the response.
Run at least 30 calls, then compute the p50, p95, and p99 of duration from those lines and compare them with the average.
Count how many calls ended with a stop reason other than a normal finish, and how many tool calls returned an error. Note whether you could have seen either number before today.

quiz.q: Users report that a service is slow, but the average response time on the dashboard is normal. Which measurement is most likely to show the problem?
options: The average latency of each server
The p99 latency of each route
The total request count per minute
The CPU usage of the application servers
quiz.explain: Latency is skewed, so a slow minority barely moves an average. A high percentile per route shows the tail and where it lives. Splitting the average per server is tempting, but each server's average hides the tail in exactly the same way.
why: An average per server still blends fast and slow requests and hides a slow minority.
Request count says how much traffic arrived, not how long anyone waited.
CPU is a cause metric; a slow dependency can make users wait while CPU stays low.

quiz.context: A customer complains that Relay replied 'I could not find your order', although the order exists. Support gives you the request ID.
options: The order lookup tool timed out and the agent answered without the order
The model invented the claim that the order did not exist
The order ID in the request does not exist in Postgres
The reply failed and the web app showed a fallback message
quiz.explain: The warning five seconds after the tool call shows the tool timed out, and the model then answered with what it had. Blaming the model is tempting, but it was never given the order. The 200 status rules out a failed request.
why: The model had no order data because the tool call timed out; its answer matched what it received.
A missing order would return a normal 'not found' result quickly, not a timeout after five seconds.
The request finished with status 200, so the web app received a real reply.

quiz.q: A teammate wants to add `ticket_id` as a label on Relay's reply latency histogram, to find slow tickets. What is the better approach?
options: Add the label, and shorten how long the metric is kept
Add the label only for replies slower than 5 seconds
Keep route as the label, and put `ticket_id` on spans and log lines
Create a separate histogram for each ticket
quiz.explain: Ticket IDs are unbounded, so any metric labeled with them creates a series per ticket. Spans and log lines carry per-request detail at no series cost, and you find slow tickets by filtering traces on duration. Shorter retention does not help, because the backend still holds every live series.
why: Retention limits history, but every active ticket still creates its own series.
Slow replies are still thousands of distinct tickets, each a new series.
One histogram per ticket is the same cardinality problem under another name.

artifact.title: A slow Relay reply
artifact.code:
start(ms)  dur(ms)  span
        0     8120  api POST /tickets/377/reply  status 200
        2       11    postgres SELECT ticket, messages
       14     8070    agent.run
       14     1180      llm.call #1  stop=tool_use
     7020     1060      llm.call #2  stop=end_turn
     8090       26    postgres INSERT message

options: The LLM provider, since both visible agent spans are model calls
Postgres, since database queries are the usual slow hop
The response serialization at the end of the handler
The tool requested by the first call, which runs with no span
quiz.explain: Inside `agent.run` there is a 5.8-second gap between the end of the first model call and the start of the second. The first call stopped with `tool_use`, so a tool ran in that gap without being instrumented. Blaming the provider is tempting, but the model spans total only about 2.2 seconds.
why: The two model calls take about 2.2 seconds together; the missing time sits between them.
The visible Postgres spans are short, and an instrumented driver would show a slow query as its own span.
Serialization happens after `agent.run` ends, and the gap is inside `agent.run`.

quiz.q: Relay keeps 5 percent of traces, chosen at random when each request starts. Engineers keep finding that the trace for a reported failure is missing. Which change addresses this directly?
options: Raise the head sampling rate from 5 to 10 percent
Switch to tail sampling that keeps every error and slow trace
Add more spans to each trace
Turn on debug logging in production
quiz.explain: Head sampling decides before anyone knows a request will fail, so failures are kept at the same low rate as everything else. Tail sampling decides after the trace ends and can keep all errors. Doubling the head rate still discards nine traces in ten.
why: At 10 percent, nine out of ten failed traces are still discarded.
More spans make kept traces richer but do not change which traces are kept.
Debug logs add volume and cost, and do not bring back missing traces.

quiz.context: Relay's reply SLO is 99.5 percent of replies good over a 28-day window. About 300,000 replies are expected in the window. With 10 days left, 1,100 replies have been bad.
options: About 400 bad replies
None, the SLO is already missed
About 1,100 bad replies
About 1,500 bad replies
quiz.explain: The budget is 0.5 percent of 300,000, which is 1,500 bad replies. 1,100 are spent, so about 400 remain for the last 10 days. The common slip is to read the number spent as the number left.
why: The SLO allows 1,500 bad replies, and 1,100 is still under that.
1,100 is what has been used, not what remains.
1,500 is the whole budget, and most of it is already spent.

quiz.context: Last month Relay's on-call engineer was paged 140 times. Nine pages matched a problem users noticed. Most of the rest were 'Postgres CPU above 70 percent' and 'worker memory above 80 percent', and they resolved on their own.
options: Raise the CPU threshold to 90 percent
Add a second engineer to share the pages
Page on the reply SLI and move resource alerts to dashboards
Add more cause alerts so problems are caught sooner
quiz.explain: The pages are cause alerts that rarely match user pain, so people stop reading them. Paging on the SLI fires when users are hurt, and the resource metrics stay available for diagnosis. Raising the threshold is tempting but keeps paging on a cause, just less often.
why: A higher threshold still pages on a cause, and will both miss real problems and fire on harmless spikes.
Sharing noise between two people halves the fatigue without fixing it.
More cause alerts add more pages that need no action.

quiz.q: Which of these should never appear in Relay's logs? Select all that apply.
options: The `Authorization` header of an incoming request
The LLM provider API key
The request ID
A customer's home address and phone number
The tool name and its duration
The model's stop reason
quiz.explain: Credentials and personal data spread to every system that copies logs and stay there for the retention period. Request IDs, tool names, durations, and stop reasons are exactly the fields that make logs useful and expose nothing about the customer.

quiz.q: Put the steps of following a slow-reply problem from alert to cause in order.
items: A symptom alert fires because the reply SLI is below target
The dashboard shows the reply route's p99 rose at 14:05, right after a deploy
You open slow traces from that route after 14:05
One span, the `lookup_order` query, dominates each slow trace
You filter logs by one trace's request ID to read the error details
quiz.explain: Each signal narrows the search for the next. The alert says users are hurt, metrics say where and since when, traces say which hop, and logs give the details. Starting with logs means reading thousands of lines with no idea which matter.

quiz.q: Match each signal to the question it answers best.
pairs: How many tool errors happen per minute?
How many jobs are waiting in the queue right now?
What is the p95 duration of LLM calls?
Which step made this one reply slow?
What error text did this request's tool call return?
quiz.explain: Counters count events, gauges report a level, and histograms keep distributions for percentiles. Traces show timing inside one request, and logs hold the event details. Reaching for logs to answer a rate question is the most common mismatch.

quiz.context: A deploy changed the `lookup_order` tool. For two days every request returned 200 and the error dashboard stayed flat, but customers kept getting replies that said 'I could not find your order'.
quiz.q: Explain why the existing monitoring missed this, and what you would instrument so it is caught within an hour next time.
rubric: Notes that tool failures were passed to the model as text, so no HTTP error or exception was recorded
Proposes a tool error counter labeled by tool name, with an alert on its rate
Proposes an outcome-based SLI or eval signal rather than status codes alone
Keeps per-request detail such as conversation ID on spans and logs, not on metric labels
Mentions deploy markers or comparing before and after the change
quiz.model: The tool's failure became a message to the model, which apologized, so every request returned 200 and the error dashboard, built on status codes, stayed flat. I would count tool calls by tool name and outcome and alert when the error share for any tool jumps. I would add an SLI on successful answers, for example replies where all tool calls succeeded, and mark deploys on the dashboard so the jump lines up with the change. Conversation IDs go on spans and log lines, not on the metrics.

quiz.context: After Tuesday's deploy, Relay's metrics backend became slow and its bill tripled.

artifact.title: Series count per metric
artifact.code:
metric                          series Mon   series Wed
http_request_duration_seconds        1,920        1,950
llm_tokens_total                        48      212,400
tool_calls_total                        60           62

quiz.q: What most likely changed on Tuesday?
options: Traffic roughly tripled on Tuesday
The scrape interval was shortened
A new model name was added to the model label
A per-conversation value was added as a label on `llm_tokens_total`
quiz.explain: Only one metric's series count exploded, by a factor of thousands, which points at a new unbounded label on that metric. More traffic or a shorter scrape interval adds samples to existing series without creating new ones, and one new model adds a handful.
why: More traffic raises sample counts, not the number of series, and the other metrics barely moved.
A shorter interval stores more samples per series; the series count stays the same.
One new model adds a few series, not 200,000.

drills.title: Replies are slow, and the dashboard is green
drills.brief: Since Monday, support has forwarded a dozen complaints that Relay takes forever to answer questions about orders. The service dashboard shows average latency and error rate unchanged for a week. Monday's deploy switched the agent to a newer model version and included a few small tool changes.

artifact.title: Service dashboard, all routes
artifact.code:
panel                       Sat     Sun     Mon     Tue
avg latency (all routes)   28 ms   27 ms   31 ms   31 ms
5xx rate                   0.1%    0.1%    0.1%    0.1%
requests                   4.02M   3.88M   4.10M   4.25M

options: Roll back to the previous model version, since it changed on Monday
Break latency down by route and by percentile
Read the transcripts of the customers who complained
Add more API pods to absorb the load
steps.explain: A service-wide average dominated by health checks can hide almost anything. Splitting by route and percentile is cheap and says whether the slowness is everywhere or in a tail. Rolling back the model is a guess that also undoes the tool changes, and would not tell you which one mattered.
steps.reveal: Only the reply route moved. Its p50 is unchanged, and its p99 jumped on Monday afternoon.

steps.q: The typical reply is as fast as before; only the tail grew. What next?
options: Compare the new model's average latency with the old one
Add more log lines to the reply handler and redeploy
Open traces of replies slower than 10 seconds since Monday
Raise the reply timeout so slow requests can finish
steps.explain: A slower model would raise the p50 too, and it did not move. Traces of the slow requests show directly which span grew. Adding logging means waiting for a redeploy when the evidence already exists.
steps.reveal: Every slow trace has the same shape: the model calls take about 2 seconds each, and one `lookup_order` call takes 8 to 9 seconds.

artifact.code:
start(ms)  dur(ms)  span
        0    13110  api POST /tickets/2291/reply
       20    13060    agent.run
       20     2050      llm.call #1  stop=tool_use
     2074     8890      tool lookup_order
     2075     8880        postgres SELECT orders
    10968     2105      llm.call #2  stop=end_turn

steps.q: You have twenty slow traces. What is the cheapest way to find what they share?
options: Read Monday's whole diff line by line
Run EXPLAIN on every query in the orders module
Ask the model provider whether the new version calls tools differently
Compare the `lookup_order` span attributes on slow and fast traces
steps.explain: Span attributes record the inputs of each call, so comparing slow and fast ones isolates the difference in a minute. Reading the whole diff or every query works eventually but searches far more than needed.
steps.reveal: Every slow span has `lookup.by=email`; fast ones have `lookup.by=order_number`. The email path was added on Monday and runs a query that scans the orders table. The new model asks for lookup by email far more often than the old one did.

steps.q: What would have caught this on Monday afternoon?
options: An alert on average latency with a lower threshold
An alert on the reply route's latency SLI or p99
An alert on Postgres CPU usage
A daily review of the 5xx error rate
steps.explain: The problem lived only in the tail of one route, so only a per-route percentile or an SLI could see it. The average and the 5xx rate never moved, and Postgres CPU is a cause metric that may or may not cross a threshold.

drills.debrief: Root cause: a new email-based lookup path in `lookup_order` ran an unindexed query, and the new model used that path often. The model looked guilty because it changed the same day, but the p50 stayed flat, which ruled out a slower model. The fix is an index for the email lookup, covered on Day 9, and an SLO alert on the reply route. The general lesson: averages over all routes cannot see a problem in one route's tail.

drills.title: The refund email that never arrived
drills.brief: Three customers say Relay told them their refund was issued and a confirmation email was on its way, and no email came. The refunds exist in Postgres. Nobody was paged. Support found the request ID `req_51c0` on one of the tickets, where Relay's web app records it.

options: Check the email provider's status page for an outage
Filter the logs on `request_id=req_51c0`
Re-send the emails to the three customers
Restart the worker fleet
steps.explain: You have the exact key for one failing request, which is the cheapest evidence available. The provider outage is a plausible story, but the logs will confirm or rule it out in seconds. Re-sending fixes three customers and teaches you nothing.
steps.reveal: The API lines show the refund, a queued email job, and a 200. Nothing from the worker matches.

steps.q: No worker line has this request ID. What next?
options: Conclude the job was never consumed and inspect the queue
Search the worker logs for the job ID `j_8812`
Turn on debug logging in the worker and wait for the next case
Check the email provider's bounce list
steps.explain: The absence of a request ID in worker logs may mean the worker never ran, or only that it does not log the ID. The job ID from the API line is a second key that tells these apart at no cost. Concluding the job was lost skips that check.
steps.reveal: The worker did run the job. It logged an error and then marked the job done, so it was never retried. Its lines carry the job ID and no request ID.

steps.q: The email has failed for two days. Why was nobody paged?
options: The paging integration must have been broken
An error-rate alert on worker logs exists but was muted
Worker alerts watch only CPU, memory, and queue depth
The worker's error lines were sampled away
steps.explain: The worker caught the exception and finished the job, so the queue drained normally and resources looked healthy. Every existing alert watched a cause, and nothing measured whether emails were actually sent. No alert was muted or broken; none existed that could fire.
steps.reveal: The worker exports resource metrics and queue depth only. There is no count of email jobs by outcome.

steps.q: Which change makes the next silent failure visible fastest?
options: Add an alert on worker CPU above 90 percent
Set the worker's log level to debug permanently
Add a nightly job that re-sends every email
Count email jobs by outcome and alert when the failed share rises
steps.explain: An outcome counter measures the symptom that matters, emails not sent, so it fires whatever the cause. CPU alerts watch a cause that did not change, debug logs add volume without alerting anyone, and blind re-sends would duplicate the emails that worked.

drills.debrief: Root cause: a template change removed a field the refund email needed, and the worker swallowed the exception and acknowledged the job. The email provider looked like the obvious suspect and was never involved. Three fixes: copy the request ID into every job and the worker's logging context, count jobs by outcome with an alert on the failure share, and let failed jobs fail so they retry or land in a dead-letter queue, covered on Day 17. The general lesson: alert on what the user should receive, not on the health of the machines that deliver it.
